name: Drones for Agricultural Monitoring 4: Precision, Climate and Livestock Monitoring
objectives: Given drone maps from more than one date and the farmer's knowledge, divide a field into two to four management zones and mark them on the ground, with each zone named and its reason stated

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Management zones: one field, different needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Divide a field into two to four management zones from a drone map and farm knowledge.
This lesson builds toward: Given drone maps from more than one date and the farmer's knowledge, you will divide a field into two to four management zones and mark them on the ground, with each zone named and its reason stated.
Most fields are not even. Soil depth, slope, old anthills, past manure, waterlogging and shade make some parts grow better than others. Precision agriculture means managing each part according to its needs.
A management zone is an area of a field that behaves the same way season after season. To draw zones, combine several drone maps (NDVI or colour, from more than one date or season) with what the farmer knows: where water stands, where the soil is shallow, where the crop always does well.
Keep it simple. Two to four zones are enough for most smallholder and medium farms: for example a strong zone, an average zone and a weak, wet zone. Name them and mark them with pegs or GPS points so workers can find them.
Step by step:
- Collect maps of the field from two or more dates if possible.
- Ask the farmer where the crop is always strong or weak, and why.
- Draw two to four zones that match both maps and farmer knowledge.
- Name each zone and mark it on the ground with pegs or GPS points.
Words to know:
- Precision agriculture: managing each part of a field according to what it needs.
- Management zone: a part of a field that behaves the same way season after season and is managed as one unit.
Try it now: Sketch a field you know (or use an example map). Draw two to four zones, name them, and write why each zone is different.
You can now divide a field into simple management zones using maps and the farmer's knowledge.

check.q: Which is a sensible set of management zones for a smallholder field?
options: A strong zone, an average zone and a weak, wet zone
check.why: Two to four simple zones are enough for most smallholder and medium farms.

check.q: The farmer says one corner always does badly, but this season's single map shows it green. What do you do?
options: Draw zones from this one map only
Check maps from other dates and seasons and use the farmer's knowledge
check.why: Zones are drawn from several maps and dates together with what the farmer knows.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Targeting inputs by zone
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Decide what each zone gets: seed, fertilizer, labour or a fix.
This lesson builds toward: For each management zone, you will decide what the zone gets: seed, fertilizer, labour or a fix, matching the action to the zone's cause and never planning drone spraying without approvals.
Once you have zones, ask what each one needs. A weak zone on shallow soil may not repay extra fertilizer; a waterlogged zone may need a drain, not fertilizer; an average zone may give the best return on extra inputs. This is variable-rate management: different rates in different places.
On large farms, machines can apply variable rates from a prescription map. On smallholder farms the same idea works by hand: workers put more or less fertilizer or manure per planting hole by zone, replant gaps only where the drone shows them, and weed or scout the problem zones first.
Some drones can spray or spread. Spraying pesticides by drone needs its own approvals from your aviation authority and your country's pesticide regulator, trained and licensed operators, and safe practices such as those in the FAO and WHO guidance on aerial application. Never spray, or advise spraying, without them.
Step by step:
- For each zone, write why it is weak or strong.
- Choose the action that fixes the cause: drain, replant, more or less fertilizer, weeding.
- Write the rate or task for each zone so workers can follow it.
- Spraying by drone: only with the required aviation and pesticide approvals.
Words to know:
- Variable-rate: applying different amounts of seed, fertilizer or water in different parts of a field.
- Prescription map: a map that tells a person or machine how much to apply in each zone.
Official sources:
- FAO and WHO: Guidance for aerial application of pesticides (2024)
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Using your zones from Lesson 1, write a one-line instruction for each zone that a farm worker could follow (for example: Zone C, wet corner: dig a drain before topdressing; no extra fertilizer).
You can now decide and write what each management zone should get, and know when spraying needs special approval.

check.q: On a large farm, what is a prescription map used for?
options: Telling machines what rate to apply in each place
check.why: On large farms, machines can apply variable rates from a prescription map.

check.q: The drone shows gaps only in the average zone. What do you tell the workers?
options: Replant gaps only where the drone shows them
check.why: On smallholder farms, workers replant only where the drone shows gaps.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Plant counts and early yield estimates
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Estimate plant stand and a rough yield range from a drone map and sample counts.
This lesson builds toward: Given a drone map and sample counts, you will calculate plant stand and a rough yield range, with the stand worked out against the target spacing and the yield given as a range.
Plant stand is how many plants came up compared with how many were planted. A drone map at fine detail shows gaps clearly. Some software can count plants automatically; you can also count by hand in sample squares on the map.
To estimate stand: mark a few sample areas of known size in each zone, count plants, and compare with the target spacing. If a maize field was planted at 75 cm by 25 cm, the target is about 53,000 plants per hectare; if you count 40,000, stand is about 75 percent.
A rough yield estimate multiplies plants per hectare by an expected yield per plant from local experience or extension figures, zone by zone. Treat it as a range, not a promise: weather, pests and harvest losses change the final number. It still helps plan storage, sales and transport early.
Step by step:
- Mark sample squares of known size in each zone on the map.
- Count plants in each square (by eye or software).
- Work out plants per hectare and compare with the target.
- Multiply by expected yield per plant from local figures to get a range.
- Write the range and what could change it.
Words to know:
- Plant stand: the number of plants that came up compared with the number planted.
- Yield estimate: an early guess of how much the field will produce.
Try it now: A maize zone of 1 hectare was planted at 75 cm by 25 cm. Your sample counts suggest 44,000 plants per hectare. Work out the stand percentage, then write what could explain the gaps and what you would check.
You can now estimate plant stand and a rough yield range by zone from a drone map and sample counts.

check.q: Why count plants in sample areas of known size?
options: To work out plants per hectare and compare with the target
check.why: Counts in areas of known size give plants per hectare, which is compared with the target spacing.

check.q: A buyer asks for your exact harvest a month before harvest. What do you give?
options: One exact number as a promise
A rough range, explaining that weather, pests and losses can change it
check.why: An early yield estimate is a range, not a promise.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Monitoring climate and environmental risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use drone flights to spot erosion, flooding and drought risk and to track climate-smart practices.
This lesson builds toward: Across a season, you will plan drone flights to spot erosion, flooding and drought risk and to track climate-smart practices, on fixed dates so maps can be compared.
Climate change brings heavier rains, longer dry spells and more heat to many farming areas. FAO describes climate-smart agriculture as farming that raises productivity and incomes, helps farms adapt and build resilience, and reduces or removes greenhouse gas emissions where possible.
Drones help on the adaptation side. After heavy rain, a flight shows gullies, washed-out terraces, silted drains and flooded plots; elevation models show where water will run next time. In dry spells, thermal and NDVI maps show which areas dry out first. Over seasons, maps show whether terraces, cover crops, mulching, tree planting and water harvesting are working.
Fly the same area on fixed dates (for example before the long rains, after the first heavy storm, mid-season, and after harvest) and compare. Share the maps with the farmer group or county or state officers: they show the whole community where to act first.
Step by step:
- Choose fixed flight dates linked to the seasons.
- After heavy rain: map gullies, washouts, silted drains, flooded plots.
- In dry spells: map which areas dry first with NDVI or thermal.
- Each season: check terraces, cover crops, mulch, trees, water harvesting.
- Compare maps over time and share them.
Words to know:
- Climate-smart agriculture (CSA): farming that raises productivity, helps farms adapt to climate change, and cuts emissions where possible.
- Erosion: soil washed or blown away by water or wind.
- Gully: a deep channel cut into land by running water.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
- FAO and ITU: E-agriculture in Action: Drones for Agriculture (2018)
Try it now: Write a yearly calendar of four climate flights for a farm you know, linked to its rainy and dry seasons. For each flight, list two things you will look for.
You can now plan drone flights that track erosion, flooding and drought risk and check whether climate-smart practices work.

check.q: After heavy rain, what does an elevation model help show?
options: Where water will run next time
check.why: Elevation models show the height of the ground, so you can see where water will run next time.

check.q: After a big storm, your maps show gullies across several farms in the group. What do you do?
options: Share the maps with the farmer group and county or state officers
Delete them because the storm is over
Fly only your own farm next time
check.why: Shared maps show the whole community where to act first.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Monitoring livestock and pasture
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a calm, safe drone flight to count animals and check pasture and water points.
This lesson builds toward: For a livestock or pasture flight, you will plan a calm, safe flight to count animals and check pasture and water points, with the herder's agreement and without scaring the animals.
On ranches and large pastoral areas, a drone can count cattle, goats or camels, find lost or sick animals, and check that water points and troughs are working, saving hours of walking or driving. Thermal cameras find animals at dawn or in thick bush.
Animals can be frightened by drones, especially at low height. Fly high enough not to scare them, approach slowly from the side, never chase or herd animals with a drone unless you are trained and it is allowed, and stop if they start to run. Ask the herder before you fly.
Pasture maps (NDVI or colour) show where grass is strong, overgrazed or bare. Over a season they help plan rotational grazing and spot land that needs rest. Never film people or homesteads without permission.
Step by step:
- Ask the herder or owner; agree time and area.
- Fly high and approach slowly from the side.
- Count animals from photos, not by circling low.
- Check water points, troughs and fences on the way.
- Map pasture: strong, overgrazed, bare.
- Stop if animals start to run.
Words to know:
- Rotational grazing: moving animals between paddocks so grass can rest and regrow.
- Overgrazing: when animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, leaving bare ground.
Try it now: Write a short flight plan for counting 60 cattle in a 40-hectare paddock: time of day, height, approach, what else you will check, and when you would stop.
You can now plan a calm, safe livestock and pasture flight and use it to support grazing decisions.

check.q: What can a drone do on a ranch?
options: Count animals and check that water points and troughs work
check.why: Drones can count animals, find lost or sick ones and check water points, saving walking or driving.

check.q: A herder is moving goats near your planned flight. What do you do?
options: Fly low to get close photos
Chase the goats into one group
Ask the herder first, fly high and approach slowly from the side
check.why: Ask the herder, and fly high and slowly from the side so the animals are not frightened.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Inspecting farm infrastructure
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Inspect dams, canals, fences, greenhouses and stores from the air and list repairs.
This lesson builds toward: For farm dams, canals, fences, greenhouses and stores, you will inspect them from the air and write a repair list, with item, location, problem, urgency and who will fix it.
Farm infrastructure is expensive and easy to forget until it fails. A short drone flight can check a water pan or small dam wall for cracks and seepage, irrigation canals and pipelines for leaks or blockages, boundary fences for breaks, greenhouse roofs and nets for tears, and store roofs for damage.
Fly slowly along the structure with the camera angled, not just straight down. Keep a safe distance from power lines and buildings, and stay within your approvals. Take photos at the same spots each time so you can compare.
Turn the photos into a repair list: item, location, problem, urgency, and who will fix it. Fly again after repairs, and before the rains when a failure would hurt most.
Step by step:
- List the structures to check and their locations.
- Fly slowly along each one with the camera angled.
- Photograph the same spots each time.
- Write a repair list: item, location, problem, urgency, who fixes it.
- Fly again after repairs and before the rains.
Words to know:
- Water pan: a dug pond that collects rainwater for animals or irrigation.
- Seepage: water slowly leaking through a dam wall or canal bank.
Try it now: Final task: write your season-long monitoring plan for a mixed farm: zones and what each gets, crop flights, climate flights, a livestock and pasture flight, an infrastructure flight, what you look for each time and what action each finding could lead to.
You can now inspect farm infrastructure by drone and plan whole-farm monitoring across a season.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Management zones No zones, or zones drawn from one map with no reason. Two to four named zones in the main field, from maps and the farmer's knowledge, with how they are marked. Uses maps from more than one date or season. What each zone gets Every zone gets the same treatment, or drone spraying is planned without approvals. Each zone has an action that fits its cause: seed, fertilizer, labour or a fix. Includes a plant stand check and a rough yield range by zone. Climate flights No climate or environmental flights. Flights on fixed dates to check erosion, flooding and drought, and what each finding would lead to. Tracks a climate-smart practice such as terraces or mulching over the season. Livestock and pasture No livestock flights, or flights that would scare animals. Flights to count animals and check pasture and water points, with the herder's agreement and safe height. Links pasture maps to a rotational grazing plan. Infrastructure Dams, fences or other structures are not included. Flights to inspect the water pan, fences and other structures, with a repair list format. Timed before the rains and after repairs, with photos from the same spots. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Which problem can a drone flight find on a greenhouse?
options: Tears in the roof plastic or nets
check.why: Flights can show tears in greenhouse roofs and nets before they get worse.

check.q: The rains start in three weeks and the water pan wall was repaired last week. What do you do?
options: Fly again to check the repair before the rains
Fly straight down only, high above it
check.why: Fly again after repairs and before the rains, when a failure would hurt most.
